--- Page 1 ---
VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations
Research
Minbo Ma1 *, Honglin Zhang1 *, Bangtao Zhou2, Chunguang Yu2,
Dasheng Ju2, Yichen Shen3, Fengli Xu1, Yong Li1 †
1Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
2Meituan, Beijing, China
3Shanghai Jiaotong University, Shanghai, China
Abstract
Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use
enable LLM agents to solve operations re-
search (OR) problems through iterative prob-
lem modeling, program construction, and ver-
ification. Yet passing self-authored verifica-
tion does not ensure that the solutions satisfy
task constraints and meet optimization qual-
ity. This gap can arise from correlated speci-
fication errors, where the generated program
and its checks share omissions or misinterpre-
tations of task requirements, alongside incom-
plete verification coverage and ineffective op-
timization strategies. We propose VERAS, a
verification-guided adaptive search harness for
reliable OR that uses verification evidence to
prioritize feasibility repair, constraint-coverage
review, and solution-quality improvement. VE-
RAS combines task-specific solution checkers
with a separate verification agent to examine
candidate solutions against the task require-
ments. It uses verification feedback to guide
feasibility repair, additional constraint check-
ing, and objective improvement, while candi-
date acceptance criteria screen revisions for de-
terioration in output validity or constraint satis-
faction. On ORAgentBench, VERAS achieves
a 42.99% pass rate, exceeding the reported
35.51% of Codex using the same LLM. Across
two industrial-scale OR problems, VERAS
reduces inter-datacenter peak bandwidth by
10.34% relative to native Codex and lowers
annualized distribution network planning costs
by 6.28% compared with expert-designed so-
lutions. Code and evidence are available at
https://github.com/holimario/VERAS.
1
Introduction
Operations research (OR) underpins decision op-
timization across diverse domains, such as trans-
portation dispatch (Vazifeh et al., 2018), energy
*Equal contribution.
†Corresponding author:liyong07@tsinghua.edu.cn
planning (An et al., 2025), and computing work-
load scheduling (Colangelo et al., 2026). Realiz-
ing these benefits requires an iterative workflow
spanning task understanding, problem formula-
tion, model solving, solution validation, and model
refinement (Williams, 2013). This iterative pro-
cess is expertise-intensive, requiring substantial
domain knowledge and optimization expertise at
each stage.
Recent advances in large language models
(LLMs) reasoning, coding, and tool use have
opened new opportunities for automated OR prob-
lem solving (Yao et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025).
Early studies focus on translating problem de-
scriptions into mathematical formulations and
solver code, supported by domain-specific train-
ing (Huang et al., 2024). Agentic systems such as
CoE (Xiao et al., 2024), OptiMUS (Ahmaditeshnizi
et al., 2024), and NEMO (Song et al., 2026) have
extended these capabilities toward end-to-end OR
solving by integrating problem modeling, program
execution, and feedback-driven refinement. In par-
allel, FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024)
and AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) leverage
evaluation-guided program evolution to discover
and improve heuristics and algorithms. While these
approaches differ in their emphasis on mathemat-
ical modeling and solver-based execution versus
algorithm design, both rely on executable programs
and iterative evaluation feedback.
The effectiveness of such refinement depends
on the reliability of evaluation feedback. When
OR agents build their own checks to verify can-
didate solutions, these self-authored verifications
may inherit the interpretation of task requirements
as the generated program. This creates the risk
of correlated specification errors, where the pro-
gram and its checks share the same omissions or
misinterpretations, allowing incorrect solutions to
pass internal verification. Figure 1 illustrates this
failure through an agent trajectory on ORAgent-

Independent verification
Figure 1: Correlated specification errors in OR agent. The optimization objective (yellow), the task constraints
(green). The solver program and its self-authored verification both omit cross-room equipment occupancy, allowing
an infeasible schedule to pass internal checks but failing in independent evaluation.
Bench (Li et al., 2026), in which both the generated
optimization program and its self-authored checks
overlook shared-equipment occupancy across op-
erating rooms, allowing the same equipment unit
to be assigned to overlapping surgeries. Such feed-
back hardly exposes the shared omission and there-
fore provides no basis for correcting it. This raises
a broader question: how can verification grounded
in task requirements guide agents to correct errors
and improve solution quality?
Addressing this question involves three chal-
lenges. First, self-authored verification is sus-
ceptible to incomplete coverage. Generated pro-
grams and verification may share specification er-
rors, leaving some task requirements unexamined
and internal verification results inconclusive. Sec-
ond, verification feedback often provides insuffi-
cient guidance for refinement. Limited diagnostic
evidence makes it difficult to distinguish modeling
errors, unverified requirements, and opportunities
for solution-quality improvement. Third, itera-
tive revisions may undermine previously veri-
fied properties. Revisions intended to repair errors
or improve the objective may introduce new vio-
lations or degrade solution quality, undermining
previously established progress.
To address these challenges, we propose VE-
RAS, a verification-guided adaptive search harness
for reliable OR problem solving. Built upon a
general-purpose coding agent, VERAS checks can-
didate solutions against task requirements using
output validity checks and task-specific solution
checkers, and conditionally invokes a separate ver-
ification agent to examine requirements beyond
existing checks.
Candidate status and verifica-
tion feedback guide feasibility repair and solution-
quality improvement through revisions to models,
algorithms, and programs. Candidate acceptance
criteria then compare output validity and checked
constraint violations with the previous candidate,
retaining the update or restoring the previous solu-
tion. These mechanisms integrate solution verifica-
tion, targeted revision, and candidate selection into
a unified solving workflow.
Our contributions are threefold:
• We identify correlated specification errors in
program construction and self-authored verifica-
tion, and introduce task-grounded verification to
expose constraint violations and coverage gaps.
• We introduce VERAS, a verification-guided
adaptive search harness that uses verification
evidence to steer OR solving refinement while
rejecting updates that worsen verified constraint
satisfaction.
• We evaluate VERAS on ORAgentBench and
two industrial OR case studies spanning heuris-
tic algorithm design and mathematical program-
ming, demonstrating improvements in task suc-
cess and solution quality.

2
Related Work
LLMs for OR Modeling and Algorithm De-
sign.
Recent LLM-based approaches to opera-
tions research (OR) have explored different ways
of constructing executable optimization programs.
In mathematical programming, CoE (Xiao et al.,
2024) coordinates specialized agents for model-
ing and code generation, while OptiMUS (Ahma-
diteshnizi et al., 2024) and OR-LLM-Agent (Zhang
et al., 2025) integrate formulation, solver execu-
tion, and iterative refinement. Another line of re-
search focuses on algorithm design, where EoH
and ReEvo employ LLM-guided evolution to de-
velop optimization heuristics (Liu et al., 2024; Ye
et al., 2024). Despite their different approaches,
both lines of work construct executable programs
that produce optimization decisions and can be it-
eratively improved through feedback.
Evaluation-Guided Program Search and Ver-
ification.
Evaluation feedback plays a central
role in refining generated programs. FunSearch
and AlphaEvolve employ automated evaluators to
guide evolutionary search toward improved algo-
rithms (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al.,
2025). In automated OR modeling, verification ad-
ditionally concerns whether generated formulations
and decisions faithfully satisfy task requirements.
NEMO employs independently generated optimiza-
tion and simulation programs for execution-based
validation (Song et al., 2026), while TriVAL and
Opt-Verifier examine modeling correctness through
stage-wise validation and complementary checks
of model structure and solutions (Fang et al., 2026;
Liu et al., 2026). ORAgentBench further assesses
end-to-end OR agents through independent evalu-
ation of decision feasibility and quality (Li et al.,
2026). These studies establish the importance of
execution feedback and verification, while VERAS
focuses on how verification evidence can guide
subsequent search. By distinguishing witnessed vi-
olations from gaps in verification coverage, VERAS
adapts program refinement and controls candidate
acceptance based on the available evidence.
3
VERAS
3.1
Overview
VERAS guides iterative OR problem solving by
distinguishing detected constraint violations from
incomplete verification coverage, thereby directing
subsequent actions toward feasibility restoration,
additional auditing, or objective improvement.
Given an OR instance I comprising a task de-
scription and instance data, we formulate the opti-
mization problem as
min
x
f(x; I)
s.t.
cj(x; I) = 1,
j ∈J ,
(1)
where x denotes the decision variables, f the objec-
tive, and cj the constraint satisfaction predicates.
As illustrated in Figure 2, a general-purpose cod-
ing agent formulates the problem, constructs an ex-
ecutable optimization program, and executes it to
produce a decision artifact. VERAS organizes this
process through three mechanisms. Task-Grounded
Verification establishes evidence of constraint vio-
lations and verification coverage. Evidence-Guided
Refinement determines subsequent solving actions
based on this evidence. Verification-filtered Update
controls candidate acceptance to preserve estab-
lished progress. At iteration t, the retained pro-
gram Pt, its decision artifact at, and verification
evidence Et constitute the incumbent state.
3.2
Task-Grounded Verification
Task-grounded verification establishes evidence of
candidate correctness by examining exported de-
cisions against the original task requirements and
instance data. For a decision artifact at, the verifi-
cation process produces
Et = Verify(I, at),
(2)
which captures structural validity, witnessed con-
straint violations, and verification coverage.
Structural Review.
The structural review estab-
lishes whether the decision artifact conforms to
the task-specific output specification. It examines
the required files, decision fields, data types, and
completeness of the submitted records. Structural
defects are reported with their affected fields or
records, providing localized feedback for correct-
ing missing or malformed outputs.
Deterministic Observer.
The deterministic ob-
server evaluates candidate decisions against task
constraints reconstructed from the task require-
ments and instance data. For each supported con-
straint, the observer computes its satisfaction status
and reports witnessed violations with affected de-
cisions and numerical residuals where applicable.
Each observer also records its verification scope,

Figure 2: Overview of the VERAS framework. A coding agent constructs and executes OR programs, while task-
grounded verification guides conditional refinement, and verification-filtered updates retain accepted candidates.
identifying the constraint families and conditions
covered by its checks. These records distinguish
observed violations from gaps in verification cover-
age and provide structured evidence for subsequent
refinement.
Isolated Challenger.
The isolated challenger ex-
tends verification by investigating requirements
that remain insufficiently examined. Operating
in a fresh context, it independently examines the
task specification, instance data, and candidate de-
cisions to search for diagnostic counterexamples.
The resulting findings supplement deterministic
observations and provide additional evidence for
subsequent program correction.
3.3
Evidence-Guided Refinement
Evidence-guided refinement employs rule-based
diagnosis and ordered conditional routing to adapt
subsequent solving actions to the candidate’s veri-
fication state.
Evidence-Based Diagnosis.
VERAS evaluates
structural validity, witnessed constraint violations,
and verification coverage to determine the next
action. The controller conditionally activates three
stages in a predefined order,
Routek(E, b) =
(
k,
gk(E, b) = 1,
skip,
otherwise,
k : restore →audit →improve,
(3)
where gk denotes the rule-based activation condi-
tion for stage k, determined by the latest verifi-
cation evidence E and remaining budget b. Each
stage is evaluated in order and skipped when its
condition is unmet. Program revisions are rever-
ified before subsequent decisions, while auditing
augments the available verification evidence.
Feasibility Restoration.
Structural defects or
witnessed constraint violations trigger feasibility
restoration. VERAS provides the coding agent
with localized diagnostic evidence, including vi-
olated requirements and available residuals. The
agent revises the mathematical formulation, heuris-
tic strategy, or program implementation to address
these defects. The revised program is executed and
reverified before candidate admission.
Coverage-Aware Auditing.
For viable candi-
dates with incomplete verification coverage, VE-
RAS invokes the isolated challenger described in
Section 3.2. Its findings supplement the verification
evidence and provide diagnostic feedback for sub-
sequent refinement. Auditing extends the available
evidence without directly modifying the optimiza-
tion program.
Performance Improvement.
Viable candidates
enter performance improvement when sufficient
budget remains. The coding agent uses accumu-
lated verification feedback to improve the original
objective f(x; I) through formulation refinement,
4


--- Page 5 ---
heuristic improvement, or additional optimization.
Each proposed revision is executed and verified
before candidate admission.
3.4
Verification-filtered Update
Verification-filtered update controls candidate ac-
ceptance by reusing the structural review and deter-
ministic observers from Section 3.2.
Candidate Admission.
For each proposed pro-
gram ePt+1, VERAS executes it to obtain a decision
artifact eat+1 and collects verification evidence eEt+1.
The admission decision is defined as
ut = Admit(eEt+1, Et, kt) ∈{0, 1},
(4)
where ut = 1 indicates acceptance and kt de-
notes the current refinement phase. Admission
requires non-regression in structural validity and
supported constraint violations. Restoration per-
mits incremental feasibility improvements, while
performance-oriented updates additionally require
valid artifacts without detected violations under
supported checks.
Incumbent Retention.
The incumbent is up-
dated according to
(Pt+1, at+1, Et+1)
=
(
( ePt+1, eat+1, eEt+1),
ut = 1,
(Pt, at, Et),
ut = 0.
(5)
Accepted candidates replace the incumbent for sub-
sequent refinement, while rejected candidates are
discarded. The retained program and its decision
artifact constitute the final output.
4
Experimental Setup
We evaluate VERAS on ORAgentBench and two
industrial-scale OR problems to assess its reliabil-
ity and optimization performance across hetero-
geneous tasks. ORAgentBench evaluates end-to-
end problem solving, while the industrial studies
examine heuristic inter-datacenter placement and
mathematical programming for active distribution
network planning.
4.1
Benchmark Study
Task.
ORAgentBench (Li et al., 2026) comprises
107 OR tasks (32 easy, 41 medium, and 34 hard in-
stances) across eight application families, spanning
static, stochastic, robust, and multi-stage optimiza-
tion. Agents construct executable optimization pro-
grams and submit complete decision artifacts from
task requirements and instance data. Multi-stage
tasks additionally require later decisions to respect
previously committed state; the benchmark reveals
the next event only after the preceding stage meets
its reward gate. Evaluation concerns the exported
decisions, rather than the plausibility of the gener-
ated formulation alone.
Agent configuration.
We use GPT-5.4 with high
reasoning effort and two concurrent task workers.
Each worker operates in an isolated environment
with Python, PySCIPOpt, and SCIP. The task-stage
wall-clock ceiling is 2,700 seconds; candidate SCIP
calls have a 300-second ceiling and a target relative
gap of 5 × 10−4. The controller reserves a fraction
of 0.30 for recovery, with a minimum recovery al-
location of 120 seconds, and allocates a fraction
of 0.22 of the remaining budget to the challenger.
These are conditional allocations, not fixed num-
bers of refinement rounds. Appendix A.3 lists the
remaining runtime settings.
Verification and scoring.
Agents receive the
public statement, instance data, and output tem-
plates, but not the benchmark evaluator or refer-
ence artifacts. Structural checks and determinis-
tic observers inspect exported decisions against
supported public constraints; the challenger sup-
plies additional diagnostic evidence. These online
checks guide refinement but do not replace the ex-
ternal evaluator. For task i, let Fi and Qi denote
its externally evaluated feasibility and normalized
quality. We report
PassRate = 100
107
107
X
i=1
I[Fi > 0 ∧Qi > 0.4]. (6)
Quality follows the benchmark’s task-specific nor-
malization against a verified reference objective
and, when available, a valid global bound. It is dis-
tinct from both the raw objective and the solver’s
reported optimality gap. Successful program execu-
tion alone does not establish constraint feasibility
or adequate normalized objective quality. Incom-
plete or infeasible submissions receive zero credit.
Overall feasibility and quality are means over tasks,
equivalent to weighting the three difficulty splits
by 32, 41, and 34; they are not unweighted means
of the split averages. For multi-stage tasks, the ag-
gregation unit is the complete required trajectory,
not an individual successful stage.

protocol, retains the original VERAS results, and
evaluates component variants in separate runs (Sec-

a repeated-run estimate of each component’s effect.
Benchmark outcomes informed harness develop-
ment; the full suite therefore serves as a develop-
ment benchmark.
4.2
Case Study: Inter-Datacenter Bandwidth
Optimization
Task.
This study optimizes the placement of
625,191 tasks across Zhongwei and Huailai, China.
Task assignments determine table locations and
cross-region transfers. The objective is to mini-
mize peak inter-datacenter bandwidth subject to
regional vCore and memory capacities; migration
volume is an auxiliary operational metric. Each
candidate is an executable placement program, not
only a saved task-to-region mapping.
Protocol.
We compare Operational Mapping,
the Historical-Majority Heuristic, native Codex,
and VERAS. Operational Mapping preserves the
archived assignments. The historical heuristic as-
signs each task to its most frequently observed exe-
cution region, defaulting to Zhongwei when no his-
tory is available. All methods use the same place-
ment constraints and bandwidth metrics. Agent-
generated programs must regenerate their assign-
ments within the 120-second dispatcher limit; this
execution limit is distinct from the agent’s search
budget.
Industrial task inputs are agent-visible but are
not redistributed; the source-replay results refer to
checks performed with those inputs available (Ap-
pendix A.5). The case uses August 2025 traces.
August 8–9 records are available for program con-
struction, while August 10 event records are ex-
cluded from agent inputs and used for evaluation.
Regional resource limits are fixed constants derived
from capacity peaks over August 7–10. Both agent
systems use GPT-5.6 Sol with xhigh reasoning ef-
fort, a timeout multiplier of three, and a 19,800-
second runtime limit. The comparison pairs an
archived VERAS run with a later native Codex run;
matching hashes establish identical task inputs and
evaluator versions. Earlier development inspected
August 10 scores, so this is a retrospective compar-
ison, not an untouched temporal test.
4.3
Case Study: Active Distribution Network
Planning
Task.
This study addresses mixed-integer second-
order-cone planning for a 54-bus active distribution
network with 63 branches, four scenarios, and 24
hourly periods. The objective minimizes annual-
ized investment, operation, and maintenance costs
through joint infrastructure and operating decisions
under electrical and operational constraints. Agents
construct executable optimization programs that ex-
port complete planning and operational decisions.
Protocol.
We compare two expert-designed mod-
els, Hourly MISOCP and Varying-Timestep MIS-
OCP, with native Codex and VERAS on the same
physical instance. Both agent systems use GPT-5.6
6


--- Page 7 ---
Sol with xhigh reasoning effort, identical task in-
puts, and the same independent evaluation protocol.
Solver execution is limited to four threads and 900
seconds. The VERAS profile has a 15,360-second
agent wall-time limit and a timeout multiplier of
two. The reported VERAS solution is a separately
selected run, rather than the VERAS arm executed
alongside native Codex.
Both reported agent solutions are regenerated
from the agent-visible task data using a stricter 750-
second solver limit. Replay time includes setup and
artifact generation, so it can exceed 750 seconds
without violating the solver limit. Replaying a
fixed program tests artifact reproducibility; it is not
a repetition of the full agent search. Independent
audits recompute constraints and objectives from
the exported decisions.
The
Hourly
MISOCP
model
uses
MAT-
LAB/YALMIP with MOSEK. It jointly optimizes
line and substation investments, discrete stor-
age/PV/wind capacities, and hourly operations
across four scenarios.
In the fault scenario,
branches 34 and 44 are disconnected during hours
7–8, with reduced substation capacities. Varying-
Timestep MISOCP adds five-minute storage charg-
ing, discharging, and state-of-charge decisions
during this window, coupled to hourly decisions
through boundary states, energy consistency, and
power headroom. It is therefore a finer-grained
operating formulation, not merely another solver
configuration for the hourly model.
5
Results and Discussion
5.1
Benchmark Study Results
On ORAgentBench, VERAS passes 46 of 107 tasks
(42.99%), exceeding the published GPT-5.4 Codex
baseline of 38 tasks (35.51%) by 7.48 percentage
points under the same official evaluation criteria
(Table 1). The largest improvement occurs on Hard
tasks, where the pass count increases from 7/34
to 12/34, while Medium performance remains un-
changed at 16/41. Mean feasibility increases from
0.57 to 0.67, accompanied by an improvement in
normalized solution quality from 0.32 to 0.39.
Execution trajectories further illustrate how task-
grounded verification supports program refinement.
Across 117 task stages, VERAS records 15 struc-
tural restorations and three reductions in witnessed
constraint residuals. In online electric-bus depot
replanning, deterministic observers identify 42 trip-
row nullability violations, all resolved through
restoration. The controller also invokes isolated
challengers for 103 tasks and admits 114 of 132 per-
formance revisions, demonstrating the integration
of independent auditing and verification-filtered
updates into the solving process.
Hard tasks remain challenging, with 17/34 pro-
ducing feasible solutions but only 12/34 satisfying
the solution-quality threshold. In addition, four
tasks fail to complete all required stages. These re-
sults highlight the distinct challenges of constraint
feasibility, solution quality, and multi-stage com-
pletion, motivating the controlled ablation study
that follows.
5.2
Ablation Study
We conduct an ablation study on six Hard tasks us-
ing GPT-5.4, comparing VERAS against four vari-
ants that disable the isolated challenger, determin-
istic observers, feasibility restoration routing, and
verification-filtered admission, respectively. VE-
RAS uses frozen results from the original evalua-
tion, while the four ablations are evaluated in sepa-
rate runs, with API-affected trials replaced based
on run validity.
Figure 3 shows that VERAS achieves the highest
task success and solution quality, passing 5/6 tasks
with a mean normalized quality of 0.621. Remov-
ing the isolated challenger reduces the pass count
from five to zero and quality to 0.054, highlighting
the importance of additional constraint auditing.
Disabling the deterministic observer reduces feasi-
ble tasks from five to four, passes from five to three,
and quality to 0.466. Without feasibility restora-
tion routing, only two tasks remain feasible and
pass, with quality dropping to 0.237. Finally, re-
moving verification-filtered admission preserves
five feasible tasks but reduces the pass count to two
and quality to 0.409, indicating its role in retaining
higher-quality solutions. Together, these results
demonstrate the complementary contributions of
task-grounded verification, evidence-guided refine-
ment, and verification-filtered updates.
5.3
Case Study: Inter-datacenter placement
Table 2 shows that VERAS achieves the lowest
peak inter-datacenter bandwidth of 1,110.603 Gbps,
reducing the peak by 10.34% compared with native
Codex (1,238.625 Gbps). Both agent-generated
programs independently reproduce their respective
archived placement outputs byte-for-byte from pub-
lic inputs within the 120-second dispatcher limit.
The expert-designed mappings exhibit substantially

Case Study: 54-bus Active distribution
network
Table 3 shows that VERAS achieves the lowest
annualized total cost of USD 39.424M/year, re-
ducing costs by 6.28% and 13.71% compared
with the expert-designed Hourly MISOCP and
native Codex, respectively.
The improvement
over the expert model is primarily driven by
lower investment costs (USD 16.154M versus
USD 18.984M), despite a slightly higher operat-
ing cost (USD 23.269M versus USD 23.081M).
Compared with native Codex, VERAS reduces
both investment and operating costs. Both agent-
generated solutions pass independent constraint
and objective audits and can be regenerated from
public inputs.

6
Conclusion
We presented VERAS, a verification-guided adap-
tive search harness for reliable operations research
algorithm discovery.
VERAS integrates task-
grounded verification, evidence-guided refinement,
and verification-filtered updates to identify con-
straint violations, distinguish gaps in verification
coverage, and guide subsequent program improve-
ment while preserving established verification ev-
idence. Experiments on ORAgentBench and two
industrial optimization problems demonstrate its ef-
fectiveness across mathematical programming and
heuristic algorithm design. These findings high-
light the importance of moving beyond pass-or-fail
evaluation toward evidence-driven search, provid-
ing a practical direction for developing more reli-
able and effective OR agents.
Limitations
Evaluation scope.
ORAgentBench informed har-
ness development, including inspection of task-
level failures. The reported aggregate is therefore
performance on a development benchmark, not an
unbiased estimate for unseen tasks or optimization
domains. Published baselines use the same scoring
criteria but were not rerun as part of this study. The
six-task ablation uses separate runs and a frozen
VERAS reference, and is too small to establish re-
liable component-level effect sizes. Shared time
ceilings also do not imply equal realized inference
compute.
8


--- Page 9 ---
Application comparisons.
The industrial stud-
ies cover one datacenter setting and one fixed
distribution-network instance. The datacenter com-
parison is retrospective: August 10 records are
withheld within runs, but earlier development in-
spected scores from that date, and resource limits
use a capacity envelope that includes it. The addi-
tional VERAS run does not preserve the archived
run’s advantage over native Codex. The grid com-
parison likewise reports a separately selected VE-
RAS run, while the expert models differ in tempo-
ral resolution. These studies demonstrate the re-
ported programs’ outcomes, rather than an average
advantage under repeated, prospectively matched
experiments.
Verification coverage.
Deterministic observers
check only implemented constraint families. A
zero residual establishes consistency with those
checks, not correctness with respect to every task
requirement. A fresh challenger context reduces
shared execution history but does not eliminate
model-level biases or guarantee that omitted con-
straints will be found. Admission filtering pre-
serves properties covered by the checks; it does
not establish monotonic objective improvement
or global optimality. Generated optimization pro-
grams still require domain-specific validation be-
fore operational use.
Reproducibility.
The experiments rely on pro-
prietary model services, and the reported source
replays reproduce fixed programs rather than entire
agent trajectories. The released industrial sum-
maries and code do not include the original oper-
ational input rows or generated decision archives,
which limits independent reproduction of the appli-
cation results. The current comparisons also do not
establish cost-effectiveness under a common token
or monetary budget.

A
Extended Experimental Details
A.1
Information Available During Evaluation
The controller revises candidates using the task ma-
terials, exported decisions, and online verification
reports. These reports are distinct from benchmark
scores. Table 4 lists the inputs and outputs of each
role. In multi-stage benchmark tasks, a stage-level
reward gate determines whether the next event is
revealed (Li et al., 2026); this does not expose the
hidden evaluator code or reference solutions to the
agent.
Table 4: Inputs and outputs of the solving and evaluation
roles. Evaluation scores a submitted artifact; it is not a
replacement for the controller’s online checks.
Role
Input and output
Producer
Task packet, prior-stage artifacts, and refine-
ment feedback; executable program and de-
cisions
Observer
Task inputs and exported artifact; structural
checks, constraint residuals, and declared
coverage
Challenger
Task packet, candidate artifact, and observer
evidence; read-only search for counterexam-
ples
Evaluator
Submitted artifact and evaluation instance;
feasibility and quality scores
On ORAgentBench, agents receive the public
statement, instance data, and output templates, to-
gether with Python, PySCIPOpt, and SCIP. De-
terministic observers check supported constraints
on exported decisions and record their scope. A
zero residual refers only to that scope. For a viable
candidate with incomplete coverage and sufficient
remaining time, the controller can request a read-
only challenger review. Final task outcomes require
completion of all mandatory stages.
In the datacenter study, August 8–9, 2025 trans-
fer records are visible to the agents, but August 10
event records are not. Resource limits are fixed
constants derived from the August 7–10 capacity
envelope. Table 2 compares an archived VERAS
run with a later native Codex run using matched in-
puts and evaluation code. The archive was selected
after earlier August 10 feedback. Thus, withhold-
ing event records within a run does not make the
development process independent of that evalua-
tion date.
For both industrial studies, agent-visible inputs
refers to data supplied to the agents during the
experiment, not necessarily data available in the
public release. Release restrictions are described
in Appendix A.5.
A.2
Prompt Construction
The initial prompt combines the task instruction, a
runtime note, and deterministic guidance selected
by public task family. Subsequent prompts are
conditional on the controller state and include seri-
alized structural audits and constraint observations.
The released harness contains the prompt text; the
descriptions below summarize its role in the search
procedure.
Feasibility restoration.
When an artifact is miss-
ing, structurally invalid, or violates an observed
constraint, the restoration prompt supplies the cor-
responding audit. It prioritizes feasibility and spec-
ifies an elastic Phase-I formulation when the ex-
act model has no incumbent. The revised artifact
is checked before it is considered for admission;
requesting a repair does not itself establish that
feasibility has been restored.
Challenger review.
The challenger operates in
a separate, read-only context.
It examines the
task specification and candidate artifact for require-
ments not adequately covered by the observers. A
counterexample report identifies the relevant rule,
affected records, observed values, and applicable
bounds. The report informs subsequent refinement
and is not treated as an external benchmark score.
Objective
improvement.
The
performance
prompt continues from the current files and
retained incumbent.
It incorporates challenger
findings and requests objective improvement
subject to recomputing constraints on the exported
artifact. The admission check evaluates structural
validity and non-regression under supported con-
straint checks. The request for a better objective
is separate from this feasibility-based acceptance
criterion, as specified in Section 3.4.
The industrial profiles add task-specific instruc-
tions to this phase. Datacenter search uses the
two visible days and examines daily peaks and
remaining resource capacity. Grid search retains
the planning decisions as optimization variables
and requires source replay under the 900-second
solver and four-thread contract. Neither addition
introduces another controller stage.
A.3
Runtime Configuration
The six-task ablation uses GPT-5.4/high, the same
2,700-second task-stage ceiling, public inputs, eval-

uator, and solver environment, with one worker per
configuration. The VERAS reference is retained
from the original evaluation. Runs interrupted by
provider limits or transport failures were selectively
rerun; completed infeasible or low-quality outputs
were retained. Equal configured limits do not imply
identical token consumption or elapsed time.
Both industrial profiles use the verification, rout-
ing, and admission mechanisms described in Sec-
tion 3.2–3.4. Relative to the benchmark profile,
they differ in model, time limits, recovery allo-
cation, challenger limits, and task-specific perfor-
mance instructions, as listed in Tables 5 and 6. The
selected grid solver leaves all eight integer deci-
sion families unfixed and uses starts derived from
the task data. The agent search budget, solver-call
limit, and end-to-end source-replay time measure
different parts of the experiment.
A.4
Solution Examples and Replay Results
A.4.1
Scenario-Dependent eVTOL Recovery
Figure 4 shows a VERAS solution for a Hard OR-
AgentBench task. The artifact contains 49 first-
stage acceptance decisions, of which 13 accept a
request. Each accepted request has one flight in
each of three weather scenarios, giving 39 flight
rows; the artifact also includes eight charging rows.
The acceptance decisions are shared across sce-
narios, whereas flight and charging schedules can
vary. The timeline observer examines 33 aircraft–
scenario timelines and reports no violations of re-
lease times, turnaround requirements, non-overlap,
or location continuity within its implemented scope.
This observation does not certify constraint fami-
lies outside that scope.

Additional VERAS run.
A new VERAS run
with the same performance instructions yields

runs and the native run satisfy the resource con-

10.34% reduction is therefore specific to the se-
lected archived run.
A.4.3
54-Bus Planning and Fault Operation
Table 3 reports a separately selected VERAS run
with annualized cost USD 39.424M. The VERAS
arm executed alongside native Codex instead ob-
tains USD 42.613M. The selected VERAS and
USD 45.690M native solutions use the same task in-
stance, LLM backend, evaluator, four-thread limit,
and 900-second solver contract; they are not out-
puts of the same paired comparison. With a 750-
second solver limit for source replay, their end-to-
end times are 829.552 and 823.924 seconds, respec-
tively. Both replayed artifacts pass the independent
constraint and objective audit.
The selected VERAS solution installs stor-
age at buses {8, 9, 13, 16, 17, 32, 50},
photo-
voltaics at {5, 8, 10, 26, 30, 33, 37}, and wind at
{12, 14, 17, 24, 39, 47}.
Figure 6 shows the in-
stalled integer units and aggregate active power
in scenario 1, converted to MW using a 10-MVA
base. Independently reconstructed load shedding
during fault hours 7 and 8 is 1.209 and 1.330 MW,
respectively.
The selected run reports a best bound of
USD 37.404M and a 5.122% solver gap for its
optimization model. This is a feasible incumbent,
not a proof of global optimality. The objective re-
constructed from the saved decisions agrees with

A.5
Released Materials and Reproducibility
The benchmark release contains task-level scores
for all 107 instances and raw event streams for
34 tasks. The application records include solver
source code, task-input hashes, and replay audits.
The manuscript project also includes aggregate dat-
acenter and grid summaries used by the case-study
plotting script. These summaries support checks of
the reported aggregate values, but do not replace
the original decision artifacts or constraint audits.
Operational input rows and generated Par-
quet/NPZ artifacts are not redistributed. Conse-
quently, independently reproducing the industrial
results requires access to the original task data in
addition to the released programs. The replay re-
sults above describe checks performed with those
inputs available; they do not imply that the public
archive alone is sufficient to rerun the applications.
14
